doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Becoming a jazz fan and musician
title: Discovering early Armstrong and working back to bop
summary: Hearing Armstrong's Hot Five solo made him seek early jazz at the library; he later loved Bird. Rowe tells of his Coltrane 'Om' mistake.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: appearing on shows and he had the handkerchief and he didn’t play much trumpet at that point and I was just kind of wondering what’s so great about this guy. I mean everybody thinks he’s so wonderful. Because “Hello Dolly” was nice but I didn’t see it as anything that really knocked me out. So I went to the local library in Jersey City, the Fine Arts Library, and I pulled out an album that had an old track of Armstrong playing “Big Butter and Egg Man From the West” with the Hot Five. And I listened to it and don’t ask me why, but as a kid I must have been 14 or 13, when he took that solo at the end of that record, after the vocal, I just perked. I just like wow, now I get it. I could see why this was great. Because I don’t think anybody else was playing like that. And I didn’t know that for a fact, because I wasn’t immersed in that time period of music, but something about it just sounded so modern and different than anything that preceded it. And the settings just seemed weird, that this archaic sounding recording had this great stuff coming out of it. And so I just started trying to find as much jazz from that time period as I could. And so, back to the Five Corners Library, pulling out more records, because you could take LPs out and you could take them home and play them and bring them back. And I had an old Wallensak open reel tape recorder, and I used to record the records after I got them and then I just played the Wallensak tapes back over and over and over again. And so my passion really became early jazz, circa 1920s, 30s, and up to the bop era. A little later I started getting into bop. But that’s how I did it. I went back to the beginning and I worked my way up to the modern jazz eventually. And you know I loved Bird when I finally heard Bird, and I didn’t find it all that radical when I heard him because I guess I’d been listening to stuff that, you know, post-bop, that was sort of in your head anyway. So I used to say I don’t know how swing people were so crazy, it sounded perfectly logical to me, what he was doing. But then I read that they weren’t happy with the bop stuff. They thought it was weird, and Chinese music Dizzy Gillespie called it, and all that stuff. But I didn’t get it. It sounded fine to me. But anyway, that was my passion. My passion was —
So you weren’t a moldy fig.
No I wasn’t a moldy fig at all. I loved bop and beyond.
It’s very curious how one thing leads to another, sometimes backwards.
I made the mistake of buying “Om” by John Coltrane when someone told me about John Coltrane. And it wasn’t the right record to get.
And so it took me some time to even put another Coltrane record on.
